First listed 2025-11-17 · episode or wrap

Inside Publishing’s Big Shakeup: AI, TikTok & the Battle Ahead | The Real Eisman Playbook Episode 34

A publishing panel explains changes in discovery, editorial labor, rights and author compensation, with Eisman mainly asking questions. The material themes are platform dependence, AI substitution of generic information, differentiated author brands and licensing economics. Verified corrections concern Amazon's generated-content policy, the distinction between training and piracy in Bartz, and author-funded costs hidden by headline hybrid royalty comparisons.

Conditional reasoning

A project without comparable history cannot satisfy the historical-comparable requirement even if its eventual quality or demand is high. The rule can therefore exclude novelty.

  • Approval requires favorable data from closely comparable prior products.
  • A novel project has no such comparable observations.

    AI-generated text, images and translations require disclosure to KDP; AI-assisted work does not. Generated content is not categorically prohibited, but must meet rights and quality rules.
  • Bartz v Anthropic order on fair use, document 231 · 2025-06-23
    Court distinguished transformative model training from acquisition and retention of pirated books. Training use received summary judgment; pirated library copies were not excused by that later use.

How he reasons here

  • Follow distribution and discovery power as formats change.
  • Separate generic information from differentiated author voice and community.
  • Do not infer legal infringement merely from technical model training.
  • Compare net contract economics after author-funded costs and rights grants.
  • Use portfolio economics for hit-driven creative businesses.
  • Historical data can screen out ideas with no close precedent.
